subject: MGMT464
title: Hurdle 2 · The Mirror Cave — Leadership Traits and Ethics

questions.stem: Identify the five Big Five personality dimensions.
options: Surgency, agreeableness, adjustment, conscientiousness, openness to experience
questions.why: The Big Five hold up across cultures. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Describe surgency.
options: Extraversion and dominance — wants to be in charge, outgoing, energetic; most linked to leadership emergence
questions.why: Surgency = extraversion and dominance. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Identify the trait most consistently linked to job performance in any role.
questions.why: Dependable, hard-working, achievement-oriented. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Explain why the chapter says traits are 'tendencies, not destiny'.
options: Behaviour can be developed regardless of personality profile
questions.why: The textbook is clear that behaviour can be developed. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Describe what too much agreeableness does to a leader.
questions.why: Helps interpersonal skill; too much and hard decisions are avoided. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Identify the trait the textbook treats as a precondition for the other eight.
questions.why: If you do not want to be a leader, you will not be an effective one. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Describe an internal locus of control.
options: Believing you control your fate and taking responsibility
questions.why: Internal vs external locus. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Identify the trait whose absence is the most cited reason careers derail.
questions.why: Insensitivity — the most cited reason careers derail. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Describe what dominance without sensitivity, integrity or stability produces.
questions.why: Dominance alone becomes bullying. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Identify the Big Five dimension that integrity maps to in the chapter table.
questions.why: Integrity — conscientiousness. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Identify McClelland's three needs.
options: Need for achievement, need for power, need for affiliation
Need for money, status and safety
Need for rest, food and friends
Need for rules, order and control
questions.why: Achievement Motivation Theory. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Describe the Leader Motive Profile.
options: High socialised need for power, moderate need for achievement, lower need for affiliation
High achievement, low power, high affiliation
questions.why: The profile matters more than any single need. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Explain why a very high need for achievement can make a poor leader.
options: The star performer prefers to do it all alone, but leadership means getting results through others
questions.why: The surprise for many students. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Differentiate socialised power from personal power.
options: Socialised power is used for the group's benefit; personal power for personal gain
questions.why: Socialised power, not personal gain. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Describe Theory X.
options: Employees dislike work, avoid responsibility and must be closely supervised and controlled
Employees like work and accept responsibility
questions.why: McGregor's Theory X. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Describe the Pygmalion effect.
options: Leaders' expectations and treatment of followers explain and predict followers' performance — the self-fulfilling prophecy
questions.why: Expect much, and people rise to it. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Identify the attitude combination the textbook calls the effective style.
options: Theory Y with a positive self-concept
Theory X with a positive self-concept
Theory Y with a negative self-concept
Theory X with a negative self-concept
questions.why: Top-left of the table. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Explain how self-concept can be built.
options: Set goals, act, succeed small, repeat
questions.why: Self-concept can be built. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Identify the three levels of moral development in order.
questions.why: Kohlberg's levels as used in the textbook. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Describe the conventional level.
options: Living up to expectations defined by others — the group, the boss, the law; most people most of the time
Universal principles regardless of the group
questions.why: 'Everyone does it' or 'my manager told me to'. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Identify the situational factors that raise unethical behaviour.
options: High reward, low chance of being caught, group approval, the leader models it, intense pressure to perform
Clear standards and rewards for honesty
questions.why: Personality decides how much situation it takes. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's answer to 'good people, bad choices' at WorldCom.
options: Both — a conventional-level person in a situation built to produce fraud
questions.why: Raise your own level AND redesign the situation. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Describe moral justification.
options: Reinterpreting immoral behaviour as serving a higher purpose — 'it is for a good cause'
questions.why: Moral justification. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Identify the rationalisation behind 'Everyone did it'.
questions.why: No single person feels responsible in a group. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Identify the rationalisation behind 'creative accounting' or 'right-sizing'.
questions.why: Cosmetic words for wrong acts. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Explain what hearing a rationalisation in your own head means.
options: It is the evidence that a line is being crossed — the arguments come after the decision
It means the decision is right
questions.why: The rationalisation is the warning. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Identify the four questions of the Rotary Four-Way Test.
options: Is it the truth? Is it fair to all concerned? Will it build goodwill and better friendships? Will it be beneficial to all concerned?
Is it legal? Is it cheap? Is it fast? Is it popular?
Will I get caught? Will I get rich? Will I be liked? Will I win?
questions.why: The Four-Way Test. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Describe the stakeholder approach to ethics.
options: Create a win–win for all relevant stakeholders, or at least make sure none is unfairly harmed — and be able to say so to each face to face
questions.why: The most complete guide. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Identify what the textbook says about rewarding behaviour as an ethical leader.
options: Reward ethical behaviour and punish unethical behaviour even when it made money
questions.why: Being an ethical leader. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Explain why integrity is a leadership trait, in the chapter's words.
options: Trust is what makes influence possible at all
questions.why: Ethics and effectiveness are not opposites. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Identify the trait described as 'adjusts to different situations; open to change'.
questions.why: Flexibility — openness. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Describe a Theory X leader with a negative self-concept.
options: Blames, does not trust or expect much of anyone
Fears being disliked but trusts others
questions.why: Bottom-right of the table. See §2.4.

questions.stem: In the Mirror Cave each rescuer sees their own nature. Classify Omar, who wants to be in charge, is outgoing and full of energy.
questions.why: Omar: 'Let me lead the way — I'll take charge of the climb!' Surgency is extraversion and dominance. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Analyse Dana, who panics and turns moody whenever the gang is near. Determine the Big Five dimension she is low on.
questions.why: Followers read the leader's mood. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Analyse Noor, who is curious about every new path and happy to try the unknown tunnel. Classify the dimension.
questions.why: Essential for the change element of leadership. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Analyse Rami, who is so eager to keep everyone happy that he refuses to choose between two routes. Determine the problem.
options: Too much agreeableness — avoiding the hard decision
questions.why: Too much agreeableness and the leader avoids hard decisions. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Classify the Crow chief, who takes charge of his gang but humiliates and bullies them.
options: Dominance without agreeableness and sensitivity — domineering
questions.why: Watch out for dominance without agreeableness. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Analyse Rami after a failed river crossing, when he says the current was bad luck. Determine the trait concern.
options: External locus of control — blaming luck instead of taking responsibility
questions.why: Internal locus takes responsibility. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Analyse a rescuer who keeps her word even when a small lie would be easier. Determine the trait and why it matters.
options: Integrity — the base of trust that makes influence possible
questions.why: Integrity; small dishonesties destroy trust. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Analyse a brilliant strategist who ignores how the team feels and loses them. Determine the chapter's warning.
options: Intelligence without people skills — insensitivity derails careers
questions.why: Intelligence; watch out for no people skills. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Classify Omar, who wants to climb the fortress wall alone to prove he is the best.
options: High need for achievement — the star performer who prefers to do it himself
questions.why: High n-Ach: prefers to do it themselves. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Analyse Dana, who avoids every argument because she wants everyone to like her. Determine the need and the leadership risk.
options: High need for affiliation — she will struggle to make unpopular decisions
High need for power — she will bully
questions.why: Lower affiliation lets leaders make unpopular decisions. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Analyse Rami, who wants to be in charge so that the team reaches Layla, sets moderate goals and accepts being disliked when needed. Determine the fit.
options: He matches the Leader Motive Profile — socialised power, moderate achievement, lower affiliation
He is a poor leader — too much power
questions.why: The profile that predicts leadership success. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Determine what the chapter predicts about delegation by a leader with very high n-Ach.
options: He will do the work himself rather than get results through others
questions.why: Leadership means getting results through others. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Analyse the Crow chief, who watches every guard closely because 'they are lazy and will run'. Classify his attitude.
questions.why: Employees dislike work and must be controlled. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Rami tells Noor 'you can find the path; I trust you', and she does. Determine the effect at work.
options: The Pygmalion effect — expectations become performance
questions.why: Expect much and people rise to it. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a leader who trusts others but not himself and fears being disliked. Classify using the attitude table.
options: Theory Y with a negative self-concept
Theory Y with a positive self-concept
Theory X with a positive self-concept
Theory X with a negative self-concept
questions.why: Theory Y / negative self-concept cell. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Determine why the Theory X guards perform worse than Rami's team, in the chapter's view.
options: They were treated as if they were lazy, so they became so
questions.why: Not because the people were lazy but because they were treated as if they were. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Classify a gang member who refuses to steal only because he fears being caught.
questions.why: 'Will I get caught?' See §2.5.

questions.stem: Classify Dana, who would take a wrong order from Rami because 'the captain told me to'.
questions.why: Living up to expectations defined by others. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Classify Noor, who refuses to leave an injured gang boy behind even though the team wants to move on.
options: Postconventional — universal principles regardless of the group
questions.why: Will break rules that violate principles. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Analyse the Crow camp: high reward, nobody checks, the chief steals openly and demands results. Determine why ordinary members turn bad.
options: The situation is built to produce unethical behaviour
questions.why: High reward, low detection, group approval, leader models it, pressure. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Classify the director's phrase 'every division does it' in the quarter-end case.
questions.why: Marking guide, task 1. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Classify 'the auditors never look'.
questions.why: Minimising the harm. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Classify the Crow chief's 'the village deserved it — they refused to pay'.
questions.why: Claiming the victim provoked it. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Classify Omar's 'I only broke the gate because Rami ordered it'.
questions.why: 'I was only following orders.' See §2.6.

questions.stem: Classify 'we only borrowed the boat; the gang does far worse'.
questions.why: Comparing to a bigger wrong. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Determine the stakeholders unfairly harmed in the quarter-end case if the manager complies.
options: Investors and auditors who are misled, and whoever later carries the blame
questions.why: Marking guide, task 3. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Select the response the marking guide accepts for the quarter-end case.
options: A respectful refusal or a lawful alternative, such as recording correctly and explaining the shortfall
Reporting the director to the press first
questions.why: Task 4: refusal or lawful alternative, worded respectfully. See §2.7.

questions.stem: The Crow chief offers Rami gold to abandon Layla. Rami asks: 'Would I want to be on the receiving end of this?' Classify the guide he is using.
questions.why: The Golden Rule. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Determine the trait the quarter-end decision requires most, according to the marking guide.
options: Integrity, supported by self-confidence and stability
questions.why: Task 4: integrity. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Analyse Rami, who praises honest scouts in public and dismisses a scout who lied even though the lie won a skirmish. Determine the ethical-leader practice.
options: Rewarding ethical behaviour and punishing unethical behaviour even when it made money
questions.why: Being an ethical leader. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Determine the two things ethical leadership is about, according to the chapter.
options: Raising your own level of moral development AND redesigning the situation for others
questions.why: Answer to question 4. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Analyse the chapter's claim about effective leaders across cultures. Determine the three Big Five dimensions they usually score high on.
questions.why: Universality. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Analyse the Crow chief, who enjoys power purely for himself. Classify his need for power.
questions.why: Socialised power is used for the group's benefit. See §2.3.
